introduction.summary: Plan a small service website around a specific customer need.
points: Start with one service and one audience.
List the questions a prospective customer asks.
Write a useful page that answers those questions.
Exercise: outline a local repair service page.

course-overview.summary: Connect useful content with the page's technical foundations.
points: Use a descriptive page title and a clear main heading.
Keep important information in readable HTML.
Build navigation from real links with meaningful labels.
Review the page on a narrow screen before publishing.

editor-setup.summary: Create a tiny project you can inspect and change confidently.
points: Create a folder with an index.html file.
Add a document title and a main heading.
Open the file in your browser and inspect the elements.
Change the heading, save the file and reload.

embedding-php.summary: Understand which part of a PHP page runs on the server.
points: PHP is executed by a configured server before HTML reaches the browser.
A PHP template can insert a value into an HTML page.
Escape untrusted text when inserting it into HTML.
Exercise: compare the template with its rendered HTML.

javascript-basics.summary: Make a small interaction respond to a deliberate user action.
points: Select a button and its associated status message.
Register a click listener on the button.
Update the message using textContent.
Exercise: make a contact prompt appear after a click.

components-databinding.summary: Use one card component for several services.
points: Store each service's title and description as data.
Pass that data to the same card component.
Use stable identifiers when rendering a list.
Exercise: change one title without changing the card layout.

reference-files.summary: Draft and inspect your first service page.

knowledge-check.summary: Check the page and programming foundations from the opening lessons.

reviews.name: Nadia Haddad
reviews.body: The service-page outline helped me turn a vague business idea into a useful page. I still need to refine the main heading.

reviews.name: Omar Saleh
reviews.body: Comparing the PHP template with browser HTML finally made the server step click. The worksheet is a useful checkpoint.

reviews.name: Leila Mansour
reviews.body: I used the card exercise for three repair services. Testing at a narrow width revealed a link label I had missed.

worksheet.title: Service page planning worksheet
worksheet.introduction: Work through these four exercises, then compare your result with the lesson examples.

sections.title: 1. Choose a service
sections.body: Pick a local service and name its intended customer. Write the customer's main question in one sentence.

sections.title: 2. Outline useful content
sections.body: Draft a descriptive title, one main heading and three sections answering customer questions. Avoid promises you cannot support.

sections.title: 3. Inspect the HTML
sections.body: Check heading order, meaningful link text and readable page content. Explain which parts would be produced by a server template.

sections.title: 4. Review on mobile
sections.body: Read the page at a narrow width. Check navigation and a contact button with the keyboard. Record one improvement and its reason.

questions.prompt: Which heading best describes a service page?
questions.explanation: A descriptive heading explains the service and helps readers recognize the page's purpose.

questions.prompt: Where is PHP in a server-rendered page executed?

options.label: Only when a search result is clicked
On the server before HTML reaches the browser

questions.explanation: A configured PHP server executes the template and sends the resulting response to the browser.

questions.prompt: Which API inserts a plain status message into an element?
questions.explanation: textContent treats the value as text rather than parsing it as HTML.

questions.prompt: What should identify repeated service cards in a component list?

options.label: A stable identifier from the service data
A new random number on every render

questions.explanation: A stable identifier lets the renderer track a service through changes in list order.

questions.prompt: Which review is most useful before publishing a service page?

options.label: Read the page on mobile and test its links and keyboard controls
Count how many animations it has
Hide the navigation on every small screen

questions.explanation: Content, responsive layout and operable controls matter more than decorative feature count.

web-design-foundations-1.summary: Start a landing page with a clear purpose and audience.
points: Name the page's audience and main task.
Write the main message before choosing decoration.
Sketch a heading, supporting text and primary action.
Exercise: outline a neighborhood workshop page.

web-design-foundations-2.summary: Guide attention with size, grouping and reading order.
points: Give the main heading the strongest emphasis.
Place supporting text close to its heading.
Make one primary action easy to find.
Exercise: remove a competing highlight from your sketch.

web-design-foundations-3.summary: Choose readable type and a consistent heading scale.
points: Use a limited set of text sizes.
Keep paragraph lines comfortable to read.
Increase line spacing for dense text.
Exercise: test your paragraph at twice its normal text size.

web-design-foundations-4.summary: Use color to reinforce meaning without relying on it alone.
points: Check the contrast of text against its background.
Pair a status color with a text label.
Give links an additional visual cue.
Exercise: review the page in grayscale.

web-design-foundations-5.summary: Apply a spacing and hierarchy worksheet to your page.

web-design-foundations-6.summary: Review the decisions behind your first page design.

reviews.name: Emma Wilson
reviews.body: Grouping each caption with its heading cleaned up my workshop page more than changing the colors did.

reviews.name: Hassan Ali
reviews.body: The text-resize exercise exposed cramped buttons in my first draft. I increased spacing and kept the labels visible.

reviews.name: Chloe Martin
reviews.body: I finally chose one primary action instead of highlighting every link. The hierarchy is much easier to follow.

worksheet.title: Landing page design review
worksheet.introduction: Work through these four exercises, then compare your result with the lesson examples.

sections.title: 1. Define the task
sections.body: Name your audience and write the one action the page should support. Sketch the main heading and supporting sentence.

sections.title: 2. Build hierarchy
sections.body: Mark the first, second and third things a reader should notice. Remove one competing highlight.

sections.title: 3. Review typography
sections.body: Read a paragraph at normal and enlarged text sizes. Check line spacing, wrapping and button labels.

sections.title: 4. Check color and spacing
sections.body: Check text contrast and review the page in grayscale. Use labels as well as status colors. Record two concrete improvements.

questions.prompt: Which element should usually have the strongest emphasis?
questions.explanation: Hierarchy should support the page's purpose and reading order.

questions.prompt: How should related headings and paragraphs be grouped?

options.label: Separate every line with a large gap

questions.explanation: Proximity helps readers understand which pieces belong together.

questions.prompt: What is a useful typography check?

options.label: Resize text and check wrapping and readability

questions.explanation: Text enlargement reveals clipping and overly tight layouts.

questions.prompt: How should an error be communicated?

options.label: Use a clear message as well as color

questions.explanation: A text message communicates meaning without requiring color perception.

questions.prompt: Which choice improves a crowded page?

options.label: Use a new font for each sentence

questions.explanation: A clear primary action reduces competing visual emphasis.

javascript-essentials-1.summary: Connect a tiny script to a plain HTML page.
points: Load your script using a script element.
Open developer tools and inspect the console.
Log a short message to verify the script runs.
Exercise: change the message and reload.

javascript-essentials-2.summary: Represent a cart item's label, price and quantity.
points: Use const when you will not reassign a binding.
Use let for a binding that changes.
Numbers support arithmetic; strings represent text.
Exercise: calculate a line total from price and quantity.

javascript-essentials-3.summary: Turn a repeated calculation into a small function.
points: Accept price and quantity as function parameters.
Return their product to the caller.
Call the function with different input values.
Exercise: check zero quantity and a normal order.

javascript-essentials-4.summary: Describe a cart with arrays and objects.
points: Use an object to group an item's related properties.
Use an array to hold several items.
Map items to their display labels.
Exercise: add an item without changing existing objects.

javascript-essentials-5.summary: Choose a message based on a simple condition.
points: Compare the cart total with a delivery threshold.
Use an if branch for the qualifying case.
Provide a clear message for the other case.
Exercise: test values below, at and above the threshold.

javascript-essentials-6.summary: Update a cart summary through the DOM.
points: Find the summary element with querySelector.
Insert plain text using textContent.
Keep the source data separate from the displayed text.
Exercise: update the total after changing quantity.

javascript-essentials-7.summary: Use a cart worksheet to test event-driven behavior.

javascript-essentials-8.summary: Check variables, functions, data and DOM updates.

reviews.name: Mina Farah
reviews.body: Testing the delivery threshold at the exact boundary caught a mistake in my condition. The three test cases were useful.

reviews.name: Oliver Reed
reviews.body: Keeping the item object separate from the displayed total made my cart example easier to change.

reviews.name: Sara Hamdan
reviews.body: I used textContent for the summary instead of building an HTML string. The event worksheet tied the earlier lessons together.

worksheet.title: Interactive cart practice
worksheet.introduction: Work through these four exercises, then compare your result with the lesson examples.

sections.title: 1. Model the items
sections.body: Create two item objects with label, price and quantity. Keep them in an array and compute each line total.

sections.title: 2. Write a calculation
sections.body: Write a function that accepts price and quantity and returns their product. Test zero quantity and a normal item.

sections.title: 3. Handle an event
sections.body: Connect a button click to a quantity change. Update a summary element using textContent.

sections.title: 4. Test boundaries
sections.body: Check the delivery threshold below, at and above its boundary. Record input, expected message and actual message.

questions.prompt: Which declaration permits reassignment?
questions.explanation: A let binding can be reassigned; a const binding cannot be reassigned.

questions.prompt: What does a return statement do?

options.label: Gives a result back to the function's caller

questions.explanation: return supplies the function result and ends that function call.

questions.prompt: Which structure naturally represents several cart items?
questions.explanation: An array holds the collection while each object groups an item's properties.

questions.prompt: Which property inserts a plain summary message?
questions.explanation: textContent updates text without interpreting the value as HTML.

questions.prompt: Which values should test a delivery threshold?

options.label: Below, at and above the boundary

questions.explanation: Boundary cases help verify the comparison's exact behavior.

responsive-css-1.summary: Start with readable content on the narrowest layout.
points: Use normal document flow for the initial layout.
Allow text and cards to wrap naturally.
Avoid a fixed page width that exceeds the viewport.
Exercise: inspect the page at 320 CSS pixels.

responsive-css-2.summary: Keep sizing flexible while bounding readable content.
points: Use relative sizes for flexible page content.
Add a maximum width for long text blocks.
Include padding in your sizing decisions.
Exercise: enlarge text without clipping card labels.

responsive-css-3.summary: Use Flexbox for a row that can wrap.
points: Display the group as flex.
Allow items to wrap when space runs out.
Use gap to separate adjacent items.
Exercise: resize a group of navigation links.

responsive-css-4.summary: Use Grid to align cards in rows and columns.
points: Define columns appropriate to the available space.
Let card content determine its own height.
Avoid a minimum column width larger than the viewport.
Exercise: compare one-column and two-column layouts.

responsive-css-5.summary: Choose breakpoints when the content needs a different arrangement.
points: Resize until the current layout becomes cramped.
Change the arrangement at that content boundary.
Test a width just below and above the breakpoint.
Exercise: inspect long card titles at both widths.

responsive-css-6.summary: Complete a responsive layout test worksheet.

responsive-css-7.summary: Review flexible sizing and responsive verification.

reviews.name: Aya Karam
reviews.body: The long-title check found an overflowing grid item at 320px. A flexible minimum fixed it without hiding the content.

reviews.name: Ben Carter
reviews.body: Testing just either side of the breakpoint caught a cramped two-column layout I had overlooked.

reviews.name: Fatima Noor
reviews.body: I used wrapping flex links instead of shrinking the labels. The navigation is now readable at narrow widths.

worksheet.title: Responsive layout test sheet
worksheet.introduction: Work through these four exercises, then compare your result with the lesson examples.

sections.title: 1. Check narrow content
sections.body: Open your page at 320 and 430 CSS pixels. Check long titles and navigation without horizontal page scrolling.

sections.title: 2. Compare arrangements
sections.body: Use one column when cards are cramped and more columns when they fit. Explain the content need behind your breakpoint.

sections.title: 3. Stress the layout
sections.body: Enlarge text, add a long title and test immediately below and above each breakpoint.

sections.title: 4. Review media
sections.body: Check that images keep their aspect ratio and fit their container. Record each tested width and any remaining issue.

questions.prompt: What should drive a layout breakpoint?

options.label: When the content needs a different arrangement

questions.explanation: A breakpoint should solve an observed content or layout problem.

questions.prompt: What helps a row of links fit a narrow width?

options.label: Giving the page a huge fixed width

questions.explanation: Wrapping preserves readable items when the row runs out of space.

questions.prompt: Which CSS layout is suited to aligned rows and columns?
questions.explanation: Grid provides a two-dimensional layout system.

questions.prompt: How should an image fit a flexible container?

options.label: Keep its aspect ratio and constrain its width
Force a width wider than the page

questions.explanation: A constrained width and preserved aspect ratio avoid distortion and overflow.

questions.prompt: Which test is useful near a breakpoint?

options.label: Check widths just below and above it

questions.explanation: Adjacent widths reveal abrupt layout or wrapping problems.

react-components-1.summary: Split a product page along meaningful responsibilities.
points: Identify the product list, card and cart summary.
Give each component a clear purpose.
Keep data shared by siblings in a common owner.
Exercise: sketch the component tree before coding.
Let a card receive its title and price as props.
Use composition for a card's optional content.
Avoid copying the same card markup for every product.
Exercise: render two cards from the same component.

react-components-3.summary: Render a product list with stable keys.
points: Map product data to card components.
Use each product's stable identifier as its key.
Do not generate a new key during every render.
Exercise: reorder the list and check the displayed products.

react-components-4.summary: Keep one source of truth for an interactive count.
points: Use state for a value changed by an interaction.
Update it through an event handler.
Derive the visible total from the current state.
Exercise: add an item without storing a duplicate total.

react-components-5.summary: Give a form clear labels and feedback.
points: Associate the visible label with the input.
Keep the entered value in the form's state.
Explain invalid input next to the form.
Exercise: preserve the value when validation fails.

react-components-6.summary: Move shared cart state to a common owner.
points: Find the nearest shared parent of the controls and summary.
Own the cart state in that parent.
Pass values and event callbacks to the children.
Exercise: update the summary from two sibling controls.

react-components-7.summary: Separate user events from external-system synchronization.
points: Handle a deliberate click in its event handler.
Use an effect to synchronize with an external system.
Clean up subscriptions when the component unmounts.
Exercise: remove an unnecessary effect for a derived value.

react-components-8.summary: Build a component that works with the keyboard.
points: Use a native button for a button action.
Keep a visible focus indicator.
Give icon-only controls an accessible name.
Exercise: operate the component without a mouse.

react-components-9.summary: Review a reusable cart with a component worksheet.

react-components-10.summary: Check component responsibilities and state ownership.

reviews.name: Nour Abboud
reviews.body: Moving the cart state to the common parent removed two competing totals in my first version.

reviews.name: James Patel
reviews.body: The effect lesson helped me recognize a calculation that belonged in rendering. There is less state to keep synchronized now.

reviews.name: Lina Youssef
reviews.body: I replaced a clickable div with a button and tested the card from the keyboard. The accessible name check was easy to repeat.

worksheet.title: Component and state review
worksheet.introduction: Work through these four exercises, then compare your result with the lesson examples.

sections.title: 1. Draw the tree
sections.body: Sketch a product list, product card and cart summary. Give each component a single clear responsibility.

sections.title: 2. Choose the owner
sections.body: Mark the common owner of cart state. Derive totals from item data rather than storing a second total.

sections.title: 3. Review interactions
sections.body: Write down the events that change state. Identify any external subscription and its cleanup.

sections.title: 4. Verify reuse
sections.body: Render two products, reorder them and operate every control by keyboard. Check keys, labels and focus visibility.

questions.prompt: What should a product card receive from its parent?

options.label: A new global variable for every label

questions.explanation: Props express the card's inputs and allow the same component to render different products.

questions.prompt: Which key should identify a product in a list?

options.label: A new random value per render

questions.explanation: Stable keys preserve identity when a list changes.

questions.prompt: Where should sibling controls keep shared cart state?
questions.explanation: A common owner gives both controls and the summary one source of truth.

questions.prompt: What is an effect suited to?
questions.explanation: Effects synchronize external systems; user actions belong in event handlers.

questions.prompt: Which element should perform a button action?

options.label: A native button with a clear name

questions.explanation: A native button provides expected keyboard and semantic behavior.

accessible-interfaces-1.summary: Review a page through the tasks people need to complete.
points: Name the page's main task.
Consider keyboard, zoom and assistive technology use.
Keep content understandable and controls predictable.
Exercise: list three ways to operate the same task.

accessible-interfaces-2.summary: Give the document a useful semantic structure.
points: Use a main landmark for the primary content.
Use headings to describe the content hierarchy.
Use links for navigation and buttons for actions.
Exercise: inspect the heading and landmark outline.

accessible-interfaces-3.summary: Follow the focus order through a form.
points: Move through controls using Tab and Shift+Tab.
Keep a visible focus indicator.
Check that every action works from the keyboard.
Exercise: open and close a dialog and check restored focus.

accessible-interfaces-4.summary: Make input requirements and errors understandable.
points: Associate labels with their form controls.
Explain a format requirement before submission.
Describe an error in text near the affected control.
Exercise: correct an invalid value without losing the draft.

accessible-interfaces-5.summary: Use a practical accessibility review worksheet.

accessible-interfaces-6.summary: Check semantics, focus, labels and readable feedback.

reviews.name: Dalia Osman
reviews.body: Following focus through the dialog exposed a missing return-to-trigger step. I added it and repeated the keyboard check.

reviews.name: Adam Wright
reviews.body: The label exercise caught a placeholder that disappeared while typing. A persistent label made the form easier to understand.

reviews.name: Mariam Fares
reviews.body: I used the review sheet alongside automated checks. Enlarged text found a clipped error that the scan did not explain.

worksheet.title: Accessibility review checklist
worksheet.introduction: Work through these four exercises, then compare your result with the lesson examples.

sections.title: 1. Inspect structure
sections.body: Check the main landmark and heading order. Confirm that links navigate and buttons perform actions.

sections.title: 2. Follow the keyboard
sections.body: Use Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter and Escape where appropriate. Check visible focus and its return after closing a dialog.

sections.title: 3. Review form feedback
sections.body: Check persistent labels, instructions and text errors. Submit invalid input, correct it and confirm your draft remains.

sections.title: 4. Stress readability
sections.body: Enlarge text and check contrast. Combine automated checks with keyboard and screen-reader review; record limitations honestly.

questions.prompt: Which element should navigate to another page?

options.label: A link with a meaningful destination
A button that hides its purpose

questions.explanation: Links express navigation and expose their destinations to browsers and assistive technology.

questions.prompt: What should happen to focus after a dialog closes?

options.label: Return to a sensible trigger or next task control

questions.explanation: Restoring focus allows the keyboard user to continue from the task context.

questions.prompt: What should identify a form field while someone types?
questions.explanation: An associated label remains available when the field contains a value.

questions.prompt: How should invalid input be explained?

options.label: A clear text message near the control

questions.explanation: Text feedback identifies the problem without relying on color and preserves context.

questions.prompt: What can an automated accessibility scan establish?

options.label: Some detectable issues, supplemented by manual review
Physical keyboard behavior on every device

questions.explanation: Automated scans cover only part of accessibility; task and assistive-technology checks remain necessary.
